title: Split Array into Consecutive Subsequences
statement:
You get an integer array `nums` whose values never decrease from left to right. Decide whether its elements can be divided into one or more subsequences so that every element lands in exactly one of them and each subsequence:

- is a run of consecutive integers, each value exactly 1 larger than the value before it, and
- holds at least 3 elements.

Return `true` when such a division exists and `false` when it does not. (A subsequence keeps the chosen elements in their original order; since `nums` is sorted, any group of values forming such a run can be taken as one.)
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every way to hand values to runs is exponential. Instead, walk the sorted values once and make the safe choice for each one. A value that can extend a run already ending at `num - 1` should do so: that never hurts, because a run that is long enough stays long enough, and the value is not needed to rescue anything else. Only when no run is waiting may the value open a new run, and then it must be able to grab `num + 1` and `num + 2` right away, or it will be stranded in a run shorter than 3.

## Approach

1. Count every value in `count` (how many copies are still unplaced).
2. Keep `tails`: `tails[x]` is how many finished runs (length 3 or more) currently end at `x`.
3. Scan `nums`. Skip a value whose copies were all used up earlier by a new run.
4. Use one copy of `num`. If some run ends at `num - 1`, move that run's end to `num`.
5. Otherwise, if copies of `num + 1` and `num + 2` remain, use them to form a new run that ends at `num + 2`.
6. Otherwise `num` cannot be placed, so return `false`. If the scan finishes, return `true`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5]`, so `count` is 1:1, 2:1, 3:2, 4:1, 5:1.

- `1`: no run ends at 0; 2 and 3 are available, so form 1-2-3 and set `tails[3] = 1`.
- `2`: its only copy is used, skip.
- `3`: one copy left; use it. No run ends at 2, but 4 and 5 are available, so form 3-4-5 and set `tails[5] = 1`.
- `3`, `4`, `5`: counts are 0, skip. The scan ends, so the answer is `true`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): two passes, each doing constant map work per value.
- Space: O(n) for the two maps.

## Pitfalls

- Prefer extending an existing run over starting a new one. Starting first fails on `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7]`, where 4 and 5 must join 1-2-3.
- When starting a run, take `num + 1` and `num + 2` immediately; a run left at length 1 or 2 cannot be checked later.
- Skip values already consumed by an earlier new run, or they are counted twice.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `count` | copies of each value not yet placed in a run |
| `tails` | number of runs (length 3 or more) ending at each value |
| `num` | the value being placed |

narration.4: First pass: count how many copies of each value there are.
narration.7: Second pass: place the values in sorted order.
narration.8: Every copy of this value was already taken by a new run, so there is nothing to place.
narration.12: Is some run waiting for num, because it ends at num - 1?
narration.13: Yes: that run no longer ends at num - 1...
narration.15: No run to extend: can num start a new run with num + 1 and num + 2?
narration.18: The new run of three ends at num + 2.
narration.20: num can neither extend a run nor start one, so no valid split exists.
narration.23: Every value found a run of length at least 3.
